sections.h2: Which Logan County office does what
sections.html:
Property tax in Logan County runs through three desks. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) appraises. The Sheriff takes payment on the current bill. The County Clerk picks up whatever is still open after April 15.

The Sheriff's Office is at 100 North Owen Street in Russellville and answers at 270-726-2244 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. A link on the county's Sheriff page leads to online payment. The PVA uses PO Box 307, Russellville, KY 42276, at 270-726-8334, and it neither sets rates nor collects tax. The Clerk's Office at 229 West 3rd Street keeps weekday hours until 4:30 and answers at 270-726-6061.

Rates come from the elected bodies that levy them: fiscal court, city councils, school boards, and districts like the extension office, library and health department. Once those rates are reported to the clerk, the bills go to print.

sections.h2: Selling a house in Logan County
sections.html:
Logan County is farm country with factories, lying against the Tennessee border. Its four cities are Russellville, Adairville, Auburn and Lewisburg. Russellville is the seat, with 7,164 people in 2020. Logan Aluminum is the largest employer, and dark fired tobacco built much of the county's early money.

The July 2025 population estimate is 28,669, up 4.5 percent since the 2020 census. Owners occupy 74.3 percent of homes, the middle home value is $164,900, and middle monthly rent is $751. The county held 12,461 housing units in 2020. Two school systems divide the county, Russellville Independent Schools and Logan County Schools, which matters to buyers choosing a side of the line.

sections.h2: How a Logan County tax bill is figured
sections.html:
Two inputs produce the bill: an assessed value from the PVA and a combined rate from each district that covers the parcel. Kentucky values real estate at what it would sell for in a voluntary sale on January 1, and farm ground can be valued by its agricultural use.

The PVA calls its online roll a working file, because appeals and assessments keep changing it. The value on that roll comes before exemptions, so subtract any exemption to find the taxable amount. Rates vary by city versus rural address, so ask the County Clerk for the exact set that applies to you.

One quirk helps buyers and sellers. If a property was bought last year, the price in the deed may stand as the listed value for the next assessment, unless the property changed. The number on a recorded deed can follow the house into future bills.

The Sheriff mails bills around the first of October. From there the state schedule moves through stages, and the amount owed rises as the calendar advances.

Logan County payment schedule
Payment windowAmount owedPaid to
Oct 1 through Nov 1Face amount minus 2 percentSheriff
Nov 2 through Dec 31Face amountSheriff
All of JanuaryFace plus 5 percentSheriff
Feb 1 through Apr 15Face plus 21 percentSheriff
After Apr 15Certificate of delinquencyCounty Clerk

A bill that has not turned up by mid-October is worth a call to 270-726-2244. Once the clerk holds it, the bill carries a recorded lien and grows by interest each month plus clerk and county attorney fees. The county attorney's first warning letter goes out by May 15, and an installment plan is still possible at that point.

Meet with the PVA first. Only owners who have held that conference may take a dispute to the clerk.

  • The roll is open to view for thirteen days beginning in early May, including Saturdays.
  • File the appeal at the clerk's office no later than the next workday after that window closes.
  • A panel of local board members hears the case between 25 and 35 days later, and the clerk sets the date.

Come with facts. Without them the panel must deny the appeal. Photos, a recent appraisal, insurance policies, construction costs, and listings or sale contracts all count as proof. Anyone paid to speak for you must be a recognized professional, such as an attorney, accountant, appraiser or broker, and must hold your written authorization. Written findings explain any change, and if you stay unhappy, the state tax appeals board is next. Skipping the local panel ends that route.

Seniors, and owners classed as totally disabled, take $49,100 off the home's assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Applications go to the Logan PVA at PO Box 307 in Russellville.

Disability filers generally reapply every year, with exceptions for service-connected veteran disability and for rulings of total, permanent disability by the federal or state retirement programs. The PVA also handles exemptions for certain religious, educational and government property.

Landowners with working acreage should raise agricultural valuation with the PVA, since the state allows farm ground to be valued by use.

Each year the clerk advertises the open bills and offers them to outside buyers. For the 2025 bills the sale was set for late July at 10:00 am in the old courthouse courtroom, after half-page notices in June and the full list later that month. Call the clerk for the date of the next one.

Buyers sign up ahead. The clerk charges $5 per prior-year bill and $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250, takes a 25 percent deposit on current-year bills, and wants full payment on prior-year ones. A winning bidder steps into the lien, and the owner pays that buyer, who may add heavy fees. State rules call for a 30-day notice from the county attorney, a second notice within 60 days if needed, and a sale date that lands three to four and a half months after the bills reach the clerk.

If your house appears on the list, call the clerk before the date. Paying first keeps the lien out of an investor's hands.

Learn the balance before you sign anything, and let the closing agent show it on the settlement statement.

  • This year's balance comes from the Sheriff at 270-726-2244.
  • Older years sit with the County Clerk at 270-726-6061, with monthly interest and fees stacked on top.
  • For an inherited or vacant house, check whose name the tax roll shows before you list it.

Many local sellers are heirs, landlords or owners of older farmhouses. Ask each office for a written payoff and the date it is good through, then give both to the title agent. The faster you learn the exact payoff, the faster you can work out what you will net. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval, so the payoff and title check are the main things left to schedule before closing.

faqs.q: Where does a Logan County owner send the property tax payment?
faqs.a: Send it to the Sheriff at 100 North Owen Street, Russellville, or use the link on the county's Sheriff page. Once April 15 passes, the bill shifts to the County Clerk at 229 West 3rd Street.

faqs.q: How big is the early-pay discount on a Logan County bill?
faqs.a: It is 2 percent, for payments made from October 1 through November 1. Face amount applies November 2 through year end, a 5 percent penalty starts in January, and 21 percent starts February 1.

faqs.q: Can I still dispute a Logan County assessment after the roll closes?
faqs.a: No. The dispute needs a PVA conference and a clerk filing by the workday after the inspection window ends. The window opens again in early May the following year.

faqs.q: Does the Logan County PVA set my tax rate or take payment?
faqs.a: Neither. The PVA only assesses value and handles exemptions. Rates come from local taxing bodies, and the Sheriff takes payment.

faqs.q: What if a Logan County tax bill is already delinquent?
faqs.a: Call the County Clerk at 270-726-6061 for a payoff figure. The bill carries a lien, monthly interest and fees, and can be sold at the clerk's tax sale if it stays open.
